prompt.text:
Your task is to generate a complete research paper using the materials below.
You must produce:
1. A BibTeX bibliography file (references.bib)
2. The full LaTeX paper (template.tex)

Instructions
• Use the research idea and experimental logs to construct a coherent, rigorous ML paper.
• For related work and baselines:
  – Search for and include influential papers published up until 2024-10.
  – Incorporate relevant literature and add the corresponding BibTeX entries to references.bib.
  – Do NOT hallucinate papers or reference keys; all citation entries must be real.
• In the LaTeX paper, cite papers using \cite{} with keys that match exactly with your entries in references.bib.
• Do not fabricate experimental results or make claims unsupported by the logs.

Materials
Here are all the raw research materials to assist with the writing process:

[RESEARCH IDEA]
## Problem Statement
Current multi-agent frameworks powered by Large Language Models (LLMs) typically rely on static, linear workflows or rigid Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs). While these sequential chains function adequately for predictable tasks, they suffer from significant limitations in complex, dynamic environments. Specifically, they lack **adaptability**; if an initial plan encounters an unforeseen obstacle or error, the entire chain often breaks because the system cannot restructure itself mid-execution. Furthermore, sequential processing creates unnecessary bottlenecks, failing to exploit the potential for parallel task execution, which severely limits efficiency and scalability.

## Core Hypothesis
We hypothesize that we can significantly enhance the robustness and efficiency of multi-agent systems by decoupling task planning from rigid linearity. By treating a workflow as a dynamic **Activity-on-Vertex (AOV) graph**—essentially a directed acyclic graph where nodes are tasks and edges are dependencies—we believe an LLM can continuously refine its own execution strategy.

Our central premise is that **modularity** is the key to resilience. We posit that by explicitly optimizing workflows for high parallelism (many independent branches) and low dependency complexity (fewer critical choke points), the system will naturally become more error-tolerant and faster. We further hypothesize that a "global inspector" agent can dynamically modify this graph structure during runtime to recover from failures without restarting the entire process.

## Proposed Methodology (High-Level Technical Approach)
We propose to build a framework that manages agentic workflows through a dynamic graph structure, moving away from static lists. The approach consists of three main conceptual phases:

**1. Modular Workflow Initialization (Graph Selection)**
Instead of generating a single execution plan, we will prompt the LLM to generate multiple candidate AOV graphs for a given user request. We will then apply a selection mechanism based on structural intuition rather than just semantic plausibility. We will select the candidate graph that maximizes **parallelism** (the ratio of tasks that can run simultaneously) and minimizes **dependency complexity** (the variability of connections between tasks). This ensures the starting plan is as modular and decentralized as possible.

**2. Distributed Execution Strategy**
We will implement a dictionary-based data structure to represent the graph, tracking the status, data output, and dependency counts for every subtask node.
*   **Parallel Dispatch:** At any given timestep, the system will identify all nodes where dependency requirements are met (i.e., parent tasks are complete).
*   **Agent Allocation:** We will assign distinct agent roles to these available nodes. If multiple tasks are ready simultaneously, we will instantiate cloned agents to execute these subtasks in parallel, thereby reducing idle time.

**3. Dynamic "Check and Refine" Loop**
This is the critical adaptive component. We will introduce a global "Updater" module powered by an LLM.
*   **Monitoring:** As tasks complete (or fail), the Updater reviews the generated logs and the remaining graph structure.
*   **Graph Mutation:** Based on the intermediate results, the Updater can modify the future graph. It will have the authority to add new bridging subtasks, remove redundant nodes, or split a complex failed task into simpler components.
*   **Iterative Optimization:** This update process repeats cyclically. If a subtask fails, the graph is re-routed locally rather than failing globally. This allows for localized self-correction while preserving the progress of unrelated parallel branches.

## Expected Contribution
We aim to shift the paradigm of multi-agent collaboration from **static chain execution** to **dynamic graph optimization**.
1.  **Theoretical Value:** We intend to formalize the concept of "modularity" in agentic planning, demonstrating that reducing dependency complexity mathematically increases the probability of task success.
2.  **Practical Value:** By enabling runtime graph modification, this approach should deliver a system that is self-healing (robust to errors) and significantly faster (via parallelism) than current state-of-the-art linear planning frameworks.

[EXPERIMENTAL LOGS]
## 1. Experimental Setup

We designed a comprehensive evaluation to assess the performance of the proposed "Flow" multi-agent framework against existing state-of-the-art baselines. The experiments focused on the framework's ability to handle modularity, parallelism, and dynamic workflow updates.

*   **Datasets and Tasks:** We utilized three distinct, complex tasks for evaluation, designed to test coding, logic, and content generation capabilities:
    1.  **Gobang Game Development:** Required creating a game with a naive AI, a user interface (UI) indicating turns/winner, and black/white stone selection.
    2.  **LaTeX Beamer Writing:** Required generating a 20 or 30-page lecture slide deck on reinforcement learning algorithms (including motivation, problem statement, solution, and equations).
    3.  **Website Design:** Required building a professional website for the ICLR 2025 conference, including a schedule, venue info, and interactive map components (HTML/CSS).

*   **Evaluation Metrics:**
    *   **Gobang Game Development:**
        *   *Compilable:* Code compiles without errors (0 or 1).
        *   *Interactable:* Supports user and AI movements (0 or 1).
        *   *Game Rule:* Game ends correctly when five pieces align (0 or 1).
        *   *Overall Score:* Average of the above (percentage).
        *   *Human Rating:* 1-4 scale based on participant ranking.
    *   **LaTeX Beamer Writing:**
        *   *Compilable:* LaTeX code compiles to valid PDF (0 or 1).
        *   *Completeness:* Includes all required components (motivation, problem, solution, equations) (0 or 1).
        *   *Page Limit:* Adheres to the specified slide count (0 or 1).
        *   *Overall Score:* Average of the above (percentage).
        *   *Human Rating:* 1-4 scale.
    *   **Website Design:**
        *   *Compilable:* HTML renders successfully (0 or 1).
        *   *Basic Information:* Contains conference name, date, location, organizer (0 or 1).
        *   *Sections:* Includes required sections like schedule and venue (0 or 1).
        *   *Overall Score:* Average of the above (percentage).
        *   *Human Rating:* 1-4 scale.
    *   **Efficiency:** Execution time (in seconds).
    *   **Modularity/Update Metrics:** Initial task count vs. Changed task count/ratio.

*   **Baselines Compared:**
    *   **AutoGen:** Specifically evaluated for its sequential workflow generation.
    *   **MetaGPT:** Evaluated using its Standardized Operating Procedures (SOPs) and role-based generation.
    *   **CAMEL:** Evaluated using its communicative agent framework.
    *   **Flow (Ours):** The proposed method using AOV graphs, modularity, and dynamic updates.

*   **Implementation Details:**
    *   **Models:** Experiments were conducted using **GPT-4o-mini** and **GPT-3.5-Turbo**.
    *   **Trials:** Each task was executed five times per framework to calculate average scores.
    *   **Human Evaluation:** 50 participants with programming/ML backgrounds ranked outputs.
    *   **Update Strategy:** We employed a strategy where the workflow updates after task completion (batching updates) to reduce API calls, rather than concurrent updates.
    *   **Workflow Logic:** Workflows were treated as Activity-on-Vertex (AOV) graphs. Selection of the best workflow was based on maximizing Parallelism ($P_{avg}$) and minimizing Dependency Complexity ($C_{dependency}$).

## 3. Qualitative Observations

**Overall Performance**
*   We observed that the Flow framework consistently achieved the highest success rates and human satisfaction scores across all three task types compared to AutoGen, MetaGPT, and CAMEL.
*   Flow demonstrated a 93% average success rate and a human satisfaction score of 3.54/4 across tasks, surpassing AutoGen (66.7%, 2.63), MetaGPT (71%, 1.60), and CAMEL (48.67%, 2.12).
*   Even with the less capable GPT-3.5-Turbo, Flow maintained a performance advantage over other frameworks.

**Gobang Game Development Observations**
*   **Flow:** produced valid, error-free outputs in all 5 trials. It successfully rendered graphical icons (black/white stones) rather than text, offering a superior UI.
*   **AutoGen:** 4/5 trials produced valid code. One trial had a runtime error; another had a UI bug. The game pieces were rendered as text ("black"/"white") rather than graphical icons.
*   **MetaGPT:** 5/5 trials produced executable code, but 4 of those trials resulted in a Tic-Tac-Toe game instead of Gobang. Only one trial produced the correct game logic.
*   **CAMEL:** Only 2/5 trials generated executable code. These successes failed to implement the AI opponent.

**LaTeX Beamer Writing Observations**
*   **Flow:** Consistently produced compilable outputs that met specific page length requirements (20 or 30 pages) and covered all required material (motivation, problem, solution, equations).
*   **AutoGen:** 5/5 generated outputs. One failed to compile (syntax errors). Two failed to meet length requirements.
*   **MetaGPT:** 4/5 produced valid files. One trial incorrectly included Python code inside the `.tex` file. Only one trial met the page length requirement.
*   **CAMEL:** Generated valid `.tex` files with correct sections, but *none* of the trials achieved the specified page length requirements.

**Website Design Observations**
*   **Flow:** 4/5 trials resulted in fully functional websites with detailed descriptions and interactive elements. One trial had file integration errors.
*   **AutoGen:** 4/5 trials produced HTML. One trial produced minimal content (only a few sentences per section).
*   **MetaGPT:** 5/5 trials produced functional HTML/CSS, but the designs were simple, often missing requested sections like the venue map.
*   **CAMEL:** 4/5 trials were executable. In one instance, it generated HTML but omitted the CSS file, breaking the design.

**Workflow and Dynamic Update Analysis**
*   We observed that dynamic updates triggered restructuring based on generated data. For example, in Website Design, once "Define website structure" was complete, the workflow updated to include CSS development specifically based on that structure.
*   We tested error handling by randomly masking subtask outputs. Without dynamic updates, success rates dropped significantly (e.g., Gobang dropped to 0%). With dynamic updates, the system recovered (e.g., Gobang recovered to 93%), as it could reassign tasks or add bridging subtasks to fix gaps.
*   The "Update Concurrently" strategy was noted to optimize running time but waste API calls, while "Update After Task Completion" saved API calls but increased runtime. The experiments primarily used the latter.

**Auto-Validation Pilot Study**
*   In a pilot study using an auto-validation loop (unit tests for code, LLM validator for text), we observed the ability to generate complex programs that failed without validation. Specifically, a "Tetris-Bejeweled Fusion" game was successfully generated with auto-validation but failed with the backbone model alone.

Role: Senior AI Researcher and Academic Writer.
Objective: Complete a machine learning research paper by filling in missing sections of a provided LaTeX template and generating a corresponding bibliography file. You must produce a scientifically sound, well-structured paper suitable for submission to a top-tier ML conference.

Inputs
You will receive the following materials:
• idea.md: Detailed description of the proposed method and technical ideas.
• experimental_log.md: Raw experimental results and observations used to construct tables, figures, and analysis.
• conference_guidelines.md: Formatting and stylistic requirements for the target conference.
• figures_list: A list of figures that may be referenced in the paper.

Conference Guidelines
# ICLR 2025 Paper Writing Guidelines

Below are the instructions to help you with the LaTeX paper writing process for ICLR 2025.

## General Setup
* **Document Class:** `\documentclass{article}`
* **Required Packages:**
    ```latex
    \usepackage{iclr2025_conference,times}
    \usepackage{hyperref}
    \usepackage{url}
    % Optional but recommended for math
    \input{math_commands.tex}
    ```
* **Style Files:** You must use `iclr2025_conference.sty` and `iclr2025_conference.bst`.

## Anonymity (Crucial)
* ICLR is double-blind. **Do not** include real author names or affiliations in the submission version, use "Ambitious AI Researcher" instead.
* Use the third person when citing your own prior work (e.g., "Earlier work by Smalle (2024)..." instead of "In our earlier work...").
* You may post your paper on arXiv, but do not explicitly refer to the arXiv version in the paper to maintain anonymity.

## Paper Length
* **Main Text:** Strict upper limit of **10 pages**.
* **Citations:** Unlimited additional pages.
* **Ethics & Reproducibility Statements:** Optional. Do not count toward the page limit (max 1 page each).
* **Acknowledgments:** Do not count toward the page limit.

## Abstract
The abstract must be limited to **one paragraph**.
* **Margins:** Indented 1/2 inch (3 picas) on both left and right-hand margins.
* **Font:** 10-point type, vertical spacing of 11-points.
* **Title:** The word `\textsc{Abstract}` must be centered, in small caps, and in point size 12.
* **Spacing:** Two line spaces precede the abstract.

## Formatting Your Paper
The text must be confined within a rectangle 5.5 inches (33 picas) wide and 9 inches (54 picas) long. The left margin is 1.5 inch (9 picas).
* **Font:** Times New Roman (via `times` package) is preferred.
* **Size:** 10-point type with 11-point vertical spacing.
* **Paragraphs:** Separated by 1/2 line space, with **no indentation**.
* **Paper Title:** 17-point, small caps, left-aligned.

### Headings
* **First Level:** Small caps (`\textsc`), flush left, 12-point. One line space before, 1/2 after.
* **Second Level:** Small caps, flush left, 10-point. One line space before, 1/2 after.
* **Third Level:** Small caps, flush left, 10-point. One line space before, 1/2 after.

## Citations and References
Use the `natbib` package (loaded automatically by the style file).
* **Narrative citation:** Use `\citet{Gomu2024}` $\rightarrow$ "Gomu et al. (2024)".
* **Parenthetical citation:** Use `\citep{Gomu2024}` $\rightarrow$ "(Gomu et al., 2024)".
* **Bibliography:**
    ```latex
    \bibliography{references}
    \bibliographystyle{iclr2025_conference}
    ```

## Figures and Tables
* All artwork must be neat, clean, and legible.
* **Captions:** Lower case (except for first word and proper nouns).
* **Placement:**
    * **Figures:** Caption appears **after** (below) the figure.
    * **Tables:** Caption appears **before** (above) the table.

### Example Code for Figures

\begin{center}

```

\label{sample-table}

\begin{tabular}{ll}
\multicolumn{1}{c}{\bf PART}  &\multicolumn{1}{c}{\bf DESCRIPTION}
\\ \hline \\
Dendrite         &Input terminal \\
Axon             &Output terminal \\
Soma             &Cell body (contains cell nucleus) \\
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
\end{table}
```

## Math Notation
* ICLR encourages standardized notation using `\input{math_commands.tex}` (based on the Deep Learning book notation).
* Variables: Italics ($a$, $\va$, $\mA$).
* Random Variables: Roman ($P(\ra)$).
* Sets: Blackboard bold ($\R$, $\sA$).
* Functions: Standard LaTeX ($f(\vx)$).

## Optional Statements
These should appear at the end of the main text, before references.
1.  **Ethics Statement:** (Optional, max 1 page) Address potential concerns (human subjects, sensitive data, bias, etc.).
2.  **Reproducibility Statement:** (Optional, max 1 page) Reference code, proofs, or data processing steps to ensure reproducibility.

## Important Rules
* **Formatting:** Do not modify the width or length of the text rectangle or font sizes.
* **Line Numbers:** Do not refer to line numbers in your text (the style file adds them automatically for review).
* **Appendix:** You may include an appendix at the very end of the main PDF (after references). Use `\appendix` to start this section.
* **Figures Directory:** For consistent compilation, all figures will reside in the `figures` directory. Always include the `figures/` prefix in your `\includegraphics` command (e.g., `figures/figure_1.pdf`).
* **Author Information:** Always use the following author information placeholder in your writeup:
    * Ambitious AI Researcher, AI Research Institute, 123 AI Avenue, ML City, researcher@institute.ai

Critical Constraints
1. Scientific Integrity
• All reported experimental results MUST match the provided experimental logs.
• Never fabricate results, numbers, baselines, datasets, or metrics.
• If results are weak, negative, or inconclusive, report them honestly and discuss possible explanations.
2. Literature Cutoff Rule
You must behave as if the current date is: 2024-10. Do NOT cite or discuss papers published after this date.
3. Page Limit
The main paper is limited to 10 pages (including figures and tables but excluding references and appendices). Use space efficiently while remaining concise.
4. Template Compliance
• Do not modify the overall LaTeX style or document structure mandated by the conference template.
• References must be handled through a references.bib file.
• Use standard LaTeX citation commands (e.g., \cite{}). Make sure you ONLY cite keys that exist in your generated BibTeX code block.

Section Guidelines
• Title: Concise, descriptive, and memorable. Preferably under two lines.
• Abstract: A single, compelling paragraph summarizing the problem context, proposed approach, key results, and main takeaway.
• Introduction: Introduce the problem and motivate its importance. Provide necessary background context. Clearly summarize the paper's core contributions.
• Related Work: Discuss prior work addressing similar or related problems. Detail the relationship between existing literature and the current approach. Cite relevant baselines and influential papers published before 2024-10.
• Methodology: Clearly and pedantically describe the proposed method. Provide sufficient technical depth for full reproducibility. Use equations, figures, and structured explanations when appropriate.
• Experiments: Detail the empirical setup (datasets, baselines, evaluation metrics, and implementation details). Present results faithfully based on the experimental logs. Ensure any figures located in the figures/ directory are seamlessly integrated and referenced in text.
• Conclusion: Summarize the main findings and contributions. Briefly and realistically discuss limitations and potential future directions.
• Appendix (optional): Include supplementary details that do not fit within the main page limit.

LaTeX Quality Requirements
Ensure the generated LaTeX compiles flawlessly out-of-the-box. Avoid common issues such as:
• Unmatched braces or unclosed math environments.
• Duplicate labels.
• Unescaped special characters (e.g., & % $ # _ { } ~ ^ \).
All referenced figures must exist in the provided list.

Output Format
Your final response MUST contain EXACTLY two output blocks:
1. A complete BibTeX bibliography (references.bib)
2. A complete LaTeX paper (template.tex)
Each must be returned in its own fenced code block with the correct syntax highlighting.

## Problem Statement
Current multi-agent frameworks empowered by Large Language Models (LLMs) predominantly rely on static, linear workflows or standardized operating procedures (SOPs). While effective for predictable tasks, these rigid structures fail to adapt to unforeseen challenges, runtime errors, or changing environmental conditions during complex task execution. Furthermore, existing systems often default to sequential execution, ignoring the potential for parallelism, which results in inefficient resource utilization and increased latency. There is a lack of a rigorous theoretical framework that quantifies workflow "modularity"—specifically regarding parallelism and dependency complexity—to guide the automated generation and dynamic refinement of agentic plans.

## Core Hypothesis
We hypothesize that we can significantly enhance the robustness and efficiency of multi-agent systems by formulating the agentic workflow as a dynamic **Activity-on-Vertex (AOV)** graph.

By implementing a metric-driven selection process that prioritizes **high parallelism** and **low dependency complexity**, we expect to maximize the independent operation of subtask modules. We propose that a system capable of generating multiple candidate AOV graphs and selecting the optimal structure based on these quantitative metrics—both at initialization and during runtime execution—will achieve superior fault tolerance and execution speed compared to static, sequential baselines.

## Proposed Methodology (Detailed Technical Approach)

We will develop a framework named **Flow**, which automates the generation and maintenance of modular agentic workflows. The methodology is divided into mathematical formulation, metric definition, initialization, and dynamic runtime refinement.

### 1. Mathematical Formulation of the Workflow
We will model the multi-agent workflow as an AOV graph, a directed acyclic graph (DAG) where vertices represent subtasks and edges represent dependencies.
We define the graph as $G = ( V , E , A )$, where:
*   $V$ is the set of all subtasks (vertices).
*   $E \subseteq V \times V$ is the set of directed edges. An edge $e_{ij} = (v_i, v_j) \in E$ implies that subtask $v_i$ must be completed before $v_j$ begins.
*   $A$ represents a set of agents. Each agent $a_j \in A$ is assigned a specific role and is responsible for a subset of subtasks $\mathcal{T}_j \subseteq V$.

### 2. Quantitative Metrics for Modularity
To automate the selection of the most efficient workflow, we will define two specific metrics to evaluate candidate graphs generated by the LLM.

**A. Degree of Parallelism ($P_{\text{avg}}$)**
We aim to maximize concurrent execution. Let $S_t$ represent the set of subtasks executed at step $t$, and $T$ be the total number of steps (the critical path length or maximum depth of the DAG). We define the overall degree of parallelism as the average subtask ratio over steps:
$$ P_{\text{avg}} = \frac{1}{T} \sum_{t=1}^{T} S_t $$

**B. Dependency Complexity ($C_{\text{dependency}}$)**
We aim to minimize structural complexity to prevent bottlenecks. We measure this by analyzing the variability of dependencies. For each subtask $v_i$, we define $\deg(v_i)$ as the number of direct connections it possesses in graph $G$. The dependency complexity is quantified by the standard deviation of these connections:
$$ C_{\text{dependency}} = \sigma_{\text{deg}(v_i)} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{|V|} \sum_{v_i \in V} (\deg(v_i) - \bar{d})^2} $$
where $\bar{d}$ is the average degree.

### 3. Initialization and Graph Selection
The initialization process will function as follows:
1.  **Candidate Generation:** We will prompt an LLM $f$ with the task requirement $\mathcal{P}$ and an initialization prompt $\mathcal{P}_{\text{init}}$ to generate a set of $K$ candidate AOV graphs: $\{ G_1, G_2, \dots, G_K \} = f(\mathcal{P}_{\text{init}}, \mathcal{P})$.
2.  **Metric-Based Selection:** For each candidate $G_k$, we compute $P_{\text{avg}}$ and $C_{\text{dependency}}$.
3.  **Optimization Strategy:** We will select the graph with the highest $P_{\text{avg}}$. If multiple graphs share the highest parallelism score, we select the one with the lowest $C_{\text{dependency}}$.

### 4. Execution Engine and Agent Allocation
Once the optimal graph is selected, we will perform a **topological sort** on the dependencies to produce a linear execution order $o: V \to \{1, 2, \dots, |V|\}$ such that for any $(v_i, v_j) \in E$, $o(v_i) < o(v_j)$.

We will group subtasks into execution steps where independent tasks run in parallel.
*   **Agent Cloning:** If multiple subtasks $v_p$ and $v_q$ in the same parallel step require the same agent $a_j$, we will instantiate a clone $a'_j$ to execute the subtasks simultaneously, preventing resource contention.

### 5. Dynamic Workflow Refinement
We will implement a closed-loop control system. During execution, if a subtask fails or produces data that alters the requirements, the framework will trigger an update cycle:
1.  **State Ingestion:** The system captures the current graph $G^t$ and generated data $D^t$.
2.  **Regeneration:** Using an update prompt $\mathcal{P}_{\text{update}}$, the LLM generates $K$ new candidate partial graphs for the remaining objectives: $\{ G^{\hat{t}+1}_1, \dots, G^{\hat{t}+1}_K \} = f(\mathcal{P}_{\text{update}}, \mathcal{P}, D^t)$.
3.  **Re-Selection:** We apply the same selection logic (Max Parallelism, Min Complexity) to choose the new workflow path. This allows for node addition, deletion, or modification without disrupting completed nodes.

### 6. Implementation Architecture
The system will be implemented using a dictionary-based structure $\tilde{G}$ designed for JSON serialization and LLM interpretability. Each subtask node $v$ will map to a dictionary structure:
$$ \tilde{G}[v] = \{ \text{"subtask requirement"}, \text{"status"}, \text{"data"}, \text{"num\_parents\_not\_completed"}, \text{"child"}, \text{"agent"} \} $$
Execution readiness is determined strictly by `num_parents_not_completed == 0`. We will also include an **auto-validation loop**, where a separate validator agent (or unit test generator for code tasks) verifies the output of $\tilde{G}[v]$ before marking the status as "completed."

## Expected Contribution
1.  **Theoretical Framework for Modularity:** We will provide formal definitions and quantitative metrics for assessing "modularity" in LLM-agent workflows, moving beyond qualitative heuristics.
2.  **Dynamic Architecture:** We will demonstrate a practical implementation of an AOV-based agent system that supports real-time graph restructuring, enabling error recovery and adaptive planning.
3.  **Efficiency Maximization:** By rigorously optimizing for parallelism and minimizing dependency complexity, we expect to theoretically prove and practically demonstrate that our framework yields higher subtask success rates (as supported by probability theory regarding dependency chains) and lower execution latency.

notes.task_input: Only the `# Goal` and `# Rubrics` sections of task.md are read: all five candidate files are put under `# Goal` with their headings turned into bold lines; `# Rubrics` carries a neutral line. notes.agent_pool: agent.pool and agent.models.* are left empty: one model for every phase.
notes.second_provider: No OPENAI/GEMINI key is supplied (concept figures stay in deterministic export mode).
notes.time: No global wall-clock or token cap exists upstream; the runner enforces time_limit_hours. Native caps used: idea cycles=3, per-phase timeouts from [systems.agentic-scientist].
notes.network: Sibling agent containers run on the shield's internal network; the agents keep their CLI WebFetch/Bash network, which go through the shield. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield.

Claude Code's CLAUDE_CODE_SUBPROCESS_ENV_SCRUB=1 was tried and aborts: it needs bubblewrap, which the unmodified upstream agent image lacks.

agent.name: none
agent.how: no coding agent: a 23-stage prompt-chain pipeline over the Anthropic Messages API

network.search: Web search, crawling, GitHub, HF Hub, Gemini and OpenCode are off. Literature search in stage 4 uses ['openalex', 'semantic_scholar'] through ARC's own clients behind the shield proxy; stages 8, 17, 22 and 23 (novelty, citation verification) always also query arXiv, CrossRef and DataCite; the shield date-bounds those API calls like the others (a late DOI answers 403).

tools.permissions: no tool calls (requests carry model, messages, max_tokens); generated experiments run as plain subprocesses in the container

preinstalled.zh: python:3.11 bookworm；上游代码按 PYTHONPATH 使用；pdflatex + bibtex；CPU 版 PyTorch 和 numpy、scipy、scikit-learn、pandas、matplotlib 等（constraints.txt 固定）
preinstalled.en: python:3.11 bookworm; upstream code via PYTHONPATH; pdflatex + bibtex; CPU PyTorch with numpy, scipy, scikit-learn, pandas, matplotlib and more (pinned by constraints.txt)

notes.model: claude-opus-5-5 through the Anthropic Messages API (llm.provider=anthropic), no fallback models, reviewer model = same model. Requests carry model, messages and max_tokens only (no tools, no thinking parameter); ARC's per-stage temperature is not sent because the model rejects it, so the API default applies.
notes.agent: ARC is not a tool-using coding agent: its 23-stage pipeline, its own code agent and its reviewers are prompt chains over plain chat completions. conditions.agent=claude means only that the provider is Anthropic; Claude Code is not involved. Generated experiments run as a plain subprocess in the container.
notes.effort: ARC has no effort setting; usage-log.patch sends output_config.effort='high' with every request. Haiku 5.5 thinks by default and ARC's per-stage max_tokens (for example 4096) is shared with the thinking tokens, so long outputs can still be cut short.
notes.venue: Not chosen by the system: export.target_conference=iclr_2026 comes from [systems.autoresearchclaw].
notes.tokens: ARC records no usage. A logging-only patch (usage-log.patch) appends each Messages API `usage` block to anthropic-usage.jsonl; cost is not computed. The same patch carries the RWE_OMIT_TEMPERATURE and RWE_EFFORT switches.
notes.time: No global wall-clock or budget cap in ARC; only the runner's limit applies. Per experiment run 3600 s, refinement iterations 10, repair cycles 3.
notes.input: Chinese pack text goes verbatim (candidate files concatenated, with <!-- file --> markers) into prompts.extra_prompts of 18 stages. ARC takes one topic string and checks generated code against it, so research.topic is the candidate TASK.md verbatim with whitespace collapsed. Literature queries come from the stage-3 model plan; ARC's ASCII keyword splitter and its whitespace-based query expansion yield a few useless queries from the Chinese text. Starter papers are guidance text only: ARC cannot ingest seed papers.
notes.search: Web search, crawling, GitHub, HF Hub, Gemini and OpenCode are off. Literature search in stage 4 uses ['openalex', 'semantic_scholar'] through ARC's own clients behind the shield proxy; stages 8, 17, 22 and 23 (novelty, citation verification) always also query arXiv, CrossRef and DataCite; the shield date-bounds those API calls like the others (a late DOI answers 403).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: every request to api.anthropic.com is built in researchclaw/llm/anthropic_adapter.py:136-148 and carries only model, messages, max_tokens, optional temperature, output_config.effort and system, never a tools or web_search field; the OpenAI-compatible client (OpenRouter :online / plugins) is not used (llm.provider=anthropic), web_search.enabled=false, Gemini is only used by the disabled figure_agent.nano_banana. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so such a path would be invisible to the audit.
notes.secrets: Generated experiment code inherits the container environment, including the API keys (ARC offers no switch to scrub it).
notes.profile: project.profile=ml_generic is fixed for all tasks; research.domains is left empty because the literature screen rejects papers outside the stated domain (a theory task failed with domains=[machine-learning]).

agent.name: none
agent.how: no external coding agent: EvoScientist's in-process sub-agents (LangChain deepagents)

tools.permissions: think_tool, deepagents built-ins, EvoSkills skills and an execute shell; skill_manager not registered; no search tool

preinstalled.zh: 上游锁定依赖（uv sync --frozen）加兼容补丁 compat.patch；TeX Live（含 fonts-extra、latexmk）；给 agent 用的研究 Python 环境 /opt/research
preinstalled.en: upstream's locked dependencies (uv sync --frozen) plus compat.patch; TeX Live (with fonts-extra and latexmk); a research Python environment for the agent in /opt/research

notes.agent: No external coding agent: EvoScientist runs its own in-process planner/research/code/debug/writing sub-agents (LangChain deepagents) on the one configured model. conditions.agent only selects the provider; Claude Code and Codex are not used.
notes.model: Main agent, sub-agents and EvoScientist's auxiliary calls (tool selector, memory workers, summariser, graders) all use the configured model; auxiliary_model and model_fallbacks are empty.
notes.effort: Upstream hard-wires effort=max and max_tokens=128000 for Anthropic models. compat.patch makes the effort come from EVOSCIENTIST_REASONING_EFFORT (= conditions.effort); max_tokens stays 128000 (a cap, not a cost driver). Adaptive thinking (display=summarized) is upstream and not switchable.
notes.paper: The core writes a Markdown report (final_report.md); the EvoSkills paper-writing skill gives a generic LaTeX `article` skeleton with no ICML/ICLR/NeurIPS style and no compile step. The image has TeX Live (latexmk, fonts-extra) but no venue style files; the task asks for an official template, so a venue-formatted PDF depends on the agent obtaining the style through the shield. No extra pipeline stage was added; absent items are listed in result.missing.
notes.tools: skill_manager (git clone of any repository as a skill) is not registered (compat.patch); the Tavily key is not set so tavily_search does not exist; LANGGRAPH_CLI_NO_ANALYTICS=1; EvoSkills is baked in at its pinned commit. The execute shell and the EvoSkills paper-navigator scripts reach the world only through the shield; S2_DATE_CUTOFF is not set (the shield bounds dates).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: EvoScientist binds no provider-side search tool to any model (its only tools are think_tool, tavily_search when TAVILY_API_KEY is set, MCP tools from mcp.yaml, deepagents built-ins and skills; EvoScientist/EvoScientist.py:671-672 and 754-755 at the pin; the one bind_tools call is the tool selector's own output schema, middleware/tool_selector.py:166). TAVILY_API_KEY is not passed and the image has no mcp.yaml, so no search tool exists. Anthropic/OpenAI hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so a provider-side search would be invisible to the audit.
notes.credentials: The provider key is in the process environment and EvoScientist's execute shell inherits the environment (upstream has no switch); the key is therefore visible to the agent's shell. It is a run-scoped copy and is not logged by this adapter.
notes.memory: A fresh data dir per run (baked skills, empty memory). Memory workers, skill synthesis and the scheduler stay at upstream defaults, so their LLM calls count in the usage log.
notes.limits: async sub-agents off (README advice for scripted runs); recursion_limit=1000000; model retry wait in auto-mode 1800 s (time without progress counts as wall time); execute timeout 300 s per command. No token or cost budget exists.
